paper.title: This Week in AI
paper._sectionKeysNote: Section keys are placeholders; read the real keys from GET /api/edition-profiles.

issue5.standfirst: Two primary studies this week expose complementary agent challenges: debate can gain from adaptive evidence handling, while tool agents still fail disproportionately when operations go wrong.

items.title: DREAM: Dynamic Resolution Assignment For Multimodal Multi-agent Debate
items.finding: Across six multimodal datasets, DREAM’s per-agent adaptive image-resolution selection and uncertainty-guided rollback improved the accuracy-token trade-off over multi-agent debate baselines by 1.5–3.2% accuracy without dataset-specific tuning.
items.boundary: The evidence is confined to six benchmark datasets and the paper’s tested model/setup; it does not establish that the gains generalize to real-world agent teams or different modalities/tasks.

items.title: UndoBench: Separating Task Competence from Recovery Capability in Tool-Using AI Agents
items.finding: Across 2,880 paired trials on 12 held-out workflows, nominal task competence was 83.54% but conditional recovery success was 46.72%; naive retry caused duplicate external effects in 53.33% of trials, showing completion scores can conceal operational recovery risk.
items.boundary: The detailed figures come from a frozen lost-acknowledgment study with two open-weight models, two frameworks, three recovery paradigms, and selected enterprise workflows; commercial-model extensions support the pattern but do not validate all deployment settings.

issue5.throughLine: The useful shift is from asking whether agents can complete tasks to measuring how they reason collectively and recover safely. Both results are controlled benchmark evidence, not proof of broad real-world reliability.
watchNext: Independent reproduction of UndoBench across more workflows and deployed tool environments.
